name: Poble Vell de Corbera d'Ebre
text: The old hilltop village of Corbera d'Ebre lay on the road junction between Gandesa and the Ebro crossings. After the Republican Army of the Ebro crossed the river on the night of 24–25 July 1938, Corbera became a front-line and rear-area target, pounded by Nationalist artillery and by the German and Italian air forces over the 115 days of the battle. Fighting swept back through it in the Nationalist counter-offensives of September–November; the British Battalion of the XV International Brigade fought its last action in the hills nearby before the Brigades were withdrawn. The inhabitants never returned: a new village was built below after the war, and the ruins were declared a Bé Cultural d'Interès in 1993 as a memorial to all victims of the battle.
look: Roofless streets climbing to the shell-scarred baroque church of Sant Pere; the 'Abecedari per la llibertat' installation, the 'Calaix de Lletres' and 'La Bota' art interventions; a plaque to the British Battalion on Carrer Hospital.
plan: Pay-to-enter site (about €3, guided visits about €10); park at the top of the old village. Combine with the '115 dies' interpretation centre, C. Freginals 18–24, which is also the network's information point.

name: Serra de Pàndols – Cota 705 memorial
text: The bare limestone ridge of Pàndols, rising to Punta Alta (Cota 705), was the southern bastion of the Ebro bridgehead. Republican troops, including Líster's 5th Army Corps and the 35th Division with the XV International Brigade, held it through August 1938 against repeated Nationalist assaults supported by massive artillery and air bombardment. Men fought on bare rock where trenches could barely be dug and the dead often could not be buried. Nearby Hill 666 was held by International Brigade units, among them the British and Lincoln battalions. The ridge remained in Republican hands until the general collapse of the bridgehead in the autumn.
look: The 'Cub per la Pau' memorial and plaques near the summit, stone parapets and scraped rifle pits, and a panoramic view over the whole Terra Alta battlefield; a separate plaque marks Hill 666 (41.03300, 0.47585).
plan: Reached by a rough forest track from the Gandesa–Pinell de Brai road, then a short walk; check track conditions and fire-risk closures in summer, and carry water.

name: Museu Memorial de la Batalla de l'Ebre (CEBE), Gandesa
text: Gandesa was the prize the Republican offensive never took: after crossing the Ebro on 25 July 1938, Republican units reached the outskirts within days but were stopped by Nationalist reinforcements, and the town became the pivot of the whole battle. The museum of the Centre d'Estudis de la Batalla de l'Ebre is housed in a former school that served as a blood hospital in 1938. Its collection of weapons, equipment, documents and photographs, with recreated trench and hospital scenes, gives the best overview of the battle, fought by roughly 80,000–100,000 men on each side, before visiting the sites in the field.
look: Permanent exhibition of over 450 m² with weapons, uniforms, models, a reconstructed trench and field-hospital ward, and audiovisuals.
plan: Avinguda de Catalunya 3–5, Gandesa; tel. 977 42 09 10. Check opening days with the town hall, and ask about guided field routes to Pàndols and Coll del Moro.
disputed: Casualty totals for the battle vary widely: Preston gives about 7,150 Republican and 6,100 Nationalist dead, Thomas 10,000–15,000 Republican and 6,500 Nationalist dead; total casualty estimates run from 50,000–60,000 to over 100,000.

name: Refugi 307, Poble-sec (MUHBA)
text: Barcelona was bombed around 200 times during the war, mostly by Italian aircraft of the Aviazione Legionaria flying from Mallorca, with German participation. The residents of Poble-sec, a working-class district near the port and the Montjuïc gun batteries, dug this shelter themselves from 1937 under the Junta de Defensa Passiva. Its roughly 200 metres of narrow vaulted tunnels had water, a first-aid room, toilets, a fireplace and a children's area. Shelters like this saved many lives during the raids of 1938, including the three days of 16–18 March, when about 1,000 people were killed. After the war it was used to grow mushrooms and later as makeshift housing.
look: About 200 m of original galleries dug into the Montjuïc slope, with benches, the infirmary and toilets, and interpretation of civil defence in the city.
plan: Carrer Nou de la Rambla 175–179. Guided visits only, run by MUHBA (usually on Sunday mornings); book ahead online. Not suitable for claustrophobes.
disputed: Death tolls for the March 1938 raids are usually given as 1,000–1,300 killed, with at least 2,000 wounded.

name: Fossar de la Pedrera, Montjuïc
text: This old quarry in Montjuïc cemetery was used as a common grave for people executed by the Franco regime after Barcelona fell on 26 January 1939, most of them shot at the Camp de la Bóta. Victims of the air raids and the city's poorest were also buried here. Lluís Companys, President of the Generalitat, was handed over by the Gestapo in occupied France, tried by court-martial and shot at Montjuïc castle on 15 October 1940; he lies in the mausoleum here. The site was made into a memorial in 1985, with columns listing the names of the executed. Nearby there are also memorials to the CNT dead, to the International Brigades and to Catalans who died in Nazi camps.
look: A quiet sunken garden in the old quarry, with stone columns listing the victims' names, the Companys mausoleum, the 'Pietat' sculpture and several other memorials along the paths.
plan: Inside Montjuïc cemetery (free, open daily); bus 21 to the cemetery gate, then follow the signs; allow time to walk the sloping paths.
disputed: Figures differ: about 1,717 executions in Barcelona are documented for 1939–52 (plaques give 1,734 for Camp de la Bóta), while some sources give around 4,000 burials in the grave, including bombing victims.

name: Turó de la Rovira anti-aircraft battery (Bunkers del Carmel)
text: The Republican anti-aircraft defence (DECA) built its main battery on this 262 m hill because it commanded the city. Four Vickers 105 mm guns, directed by acoustic locators and searchlights, fired on the Italian and German bombers raiding Barcelona in 1937–38. The guns were disabled as the Republicans withdrew on 25–26 January 1939, just before Nationalist troops entered the city. After the war the emplacements were taken over by shanty housing, which remained until 1990. In 2011 the Barcelona History Museum (MUHBA) restored the site as a place explaining both chapters of its history.
look: Concrete gun platforms, the command post and barrack foundations, shanty-town floor tiles, and a 360° view over Barcelona.
plan: Free, open-air site; steep walk up from Carrer Marià Labèrnia (buses V17/22/119 go close). Busy at sunset; the small MUHBA interpretation space has limited opening hours.

name: Plaça de Sant Felip Neri (bombing of 30 January 1938)
text: On 30 January 1938 Italian aircraft from Mallorca bombed the old city of Barcelona. One bomb fell on this small square, where the church crypt was used as an air-raid shelter by the neighbouring school and children who had been evacuated from Madrid. As rescuers dug survivors out of the rubble, a second bomb struck. Forty-two people were killed, most of them children, making it one of the deadliest single incidents of the city's bombing. For decades the damage to the church front was said to come from executions; today a plaque records the true cause.
look: The church façade is still pitted with shrapnel scars, and a plaque remembers the victims; the rest of the square is unchanged.
plan: Free, always accessible, in the Gothic Quarter a few minutes from the cathedral; a quiet place, so please be respectful as the school still uses the square.

name: MUME – Museu Memorial de l'Exili, La Jonquera
text: As Nationalist forces overran Catalonia after the fall of Barcelona on 26 January 1939, a huge mass of civilians and defeated soldiers fled north to the French border: the Retirada. They crossed at Le Perthus/La Jonquera, Portbou, Coll d'Ares and the mountain passes, in winter, under air attack. France held many of them in improvised camps on the beaches such as Argelès and Saint-Cyprien. The MUME, opened in 2008 in the frontier town of La Jonquera, tells the story of this exodus and of the Republican exile: the camps, return, deportation to Nazi camps, and life abroad.
look: Permanent exhibition on the Retirada, the French camps and exile, with photographs, objects and testimonies; temporary exhibitions and a documentation centre.
plan: Carrer Major 43–47, La Jonquera; closed on Mondays; see museuexili.cat for hours and prices. The museum can advise on the exile walking routes over the nearby passes.
disputed: Estimates of the number who crossed into France in early 1939 range from about 450,000 to 500,000.

name: Castell de Sant Ferran, Figueres (last Cortes)
text: As Catalonia collapsed, the Republican government withdrew to Figueres. On 1 February 1939 Prime Minister Juan Negrín held the last session of the Republican Cortes on Spanish soil in the stables of this huge 18th-century fortress, proposing peace conditions that Franco ignored. The castle and places nearby also sheltered art evacuated from the Prado and other collections before it was sent to Geneva. Days later the government crossed into France and Nationalist troops reached the border on 10 February. From 1940 to 1942 the Franco regime used the castle as a concentration camp for Republicans returned from France.
look: One of the largest bastioned fortresses in Europe: the stables where the Cortes met, the parade ground, bastions and underground cisterns.
plan: On the edge of Figueres, 20 minutes' walk from the Dalí Museum; entry fee; check seasonal hours. Guided visits to the underground cisterns go by boat or 4x4 and must be booked.

name: Les Devees trenches, La Fatarella
text: The Serra de la Fatarella was the northern shoulder of the Republican Ebro bridgehead and its last stronghold. Les Devees was a rear position guarding the approach to La Fatarella. Soldiers built two shelters here, one in an old lime kiln, joined to a zig-zag trench on higher ground. In mid-November 1938 the final Nationalist offensive broke through at La Fatarella. The last Republican units recrossed the river at Flix on 16 November, ending the battle. The La Fatarella interpretation centre 'Internacionals a l'Ebre' tells the story of the foreign volunteers.
look: Two restored shelters, one built into a lime kiln, and about 20 m of zig-zag trench, with information panels.
plan: Signposted from La Fatarella; free, open-air site. A 12 km circular route (Ruta de Sant Bertomeu) links it with the Camposines memorial.

name: Memorial de les Camposines
text: The Camposines crossroads, on the road from the Ebro crossings at Ascó and Flix towards Gandesa, was a key junction behind the Republican front and was fought over in the final weeks of the battle. In 2009 the Generalitat built a memorial here over the line of an old trench. It is an ossuary for the remains of soldiers still being found across the battlefield, from both armies, whose identities are mostly unknown. It is the main place of remembrance for the tens of thousands who died in the battle.
look: A modern memorial building with an ossuary, beside the hermitage of Sant Bartomeu de les Camposines, and a panoramic view towards the Ebro valley.
plan: Beside the C-43 road junction between Ascó and Corbera d'Ebre; roadside parking; free.

name: Vilalba dels Arcs: Els Barrancs trenches & Mirador del Bassot
text: Vilalba dels Arcs lay on the northern edge of the Republican advance of 25 July 1938. Republican attacks failed to take the village and its hills. The Mirador del Bassot looks out from the defensive positions of the first days over the ground where those assaults were made. Just outside the village, the Els Barrancs site keeps about 700 m of trench line with firing pits, shelters and huts, the best-preserved trench network in the Ebro heritage network. The 'Soldats a les trinxeres' interpretation centre in the village explains the everyday life of the soldiers at the front.
look: About 700 m of restored trenches, firing pits, shelters and huts at Els Barrancs; a viewpoint with panels in the village.
plan: Start at the interpretation centre in the village; the Barrancs trenches are a short walk or drive away. Check hours with the Espais de la Batalla de l'Ebre network.
disputed: Coordinates are for the Mirador del Bassot in the village; the exact location of the Barrancs trench line was not verified. Sources are unclear on which army built the Barrancs trenches.

name: Quatre Camins – Cota 427 cross, Vilalba dels Arcs
text: At the Quatre Camins crossroads (Cota 427), south of Vilalba, the Catalan Carlist volunteers of the Tercio de Requetés de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat held a Nationalist position facing the Republican 31st Mixed Brigade on Punta Targa (Cota 481), only about 250 m away. On 19 August 1938 the requetés attacked towards Punta Targa and lost 58 killed and 174 wounded, according to the unit's figures; Republican losses are not recorded. This small site is a reminder that Catalans fought on both sides of the battle.
look: A memorial cross at the crossroads, with the facing hills of Punta Targa in view.
plan: Roadside site south of Vilalba dels Arcs; free; combine with the Barrancs trenches and the Montserrat crypt of the same unit.

name: Coll del Moro – Franco's observation post, Gandesa
text: From this 470 m hill west of Gandesa, on top of an Iberian settlement and necropolis, the Nationalist command watched the Battle of the Ebro. Franco himself came here, as did senior commanders and foreign military observers. The Nationalists' approach relied on artillery and air superiority to wear down the Republican bridgehead in a series of costly counter-offensives rather than seeking manoeuvre. From the observation post the whole southern battlefield is visible, from Gandesa to the Pàndols and Cavalls ridges.
look: The Nationalist observation post and its surroundings alongside the excavated Iberian tower and settlement; wide views over the Terra Alta battlefield.
plan: Beside the N-420 at km 795.5; the Iberian site is visited by reservation only (reservesmonuments.acdpc@gencat.cat, tel. 977 638 556).

name: Refugi antiaeri de Flix
text: Flix had a large chemical factory and a river crossing, and was bombed repeatedly. Its inhabitants dug this shelter under the old town. On 25 July 1938 Republican units of the XV Army Corps crossed the Ebro in the Flix–Ascó sector at the start of the offensive. On the night of 15–16 November the last Republican troops withdrew back across the river here, ending the Battle of the Ebro. Opened as a museum in 2008, the shelter is part of the Espais de la Batalla de l'Ebre network.
look: Restored shelter galleries beneath the old town, with an exhibition on the bombing of Flix and civil defence.
plan: Carrer del Castell; guided visits only, arranged through Flix tourist office or the Ebro network; wear sensible shoes.

name: Castell de Miravet – Ebro crossing viewpoint
text: The Templar castle of Miravet stands above one of the stretches where the Army of the Ebro crossed the river by boat and footbridge in the early hours of 25 July 1938. It took the Nationalists by surprise. The Republican aim was to relieve pressure on Valencia and restore the link with the central zone, and the attack advanced up to 20–40 km in the first days. The castle now holds one of the network's interpretation exhibitions on the objectives and course of the battle, and it gives a good view of how the river shaped the fighting.
look: A 12th–13th century Templar castle with a permanent exhibition on the Battle of the Ebro, and views over the river, the ferry and the village.
plan: Tue–Sat 10:00–17:30 (to 19:00 May–Sep), Sun 10:00–15:00, closed Mondays; €7 (reduced €5). The traditional river ferry (pas de barca) below the village is worth combining with a visit.

name: Castell de Móra d'Ebre
text: Móra d'Ebre, with its road bridge and the pontoon bridges thrown across the river after 25 July 1938, was the main supply artery of the Republican bridgehead. That made it a constant target for the Nationalist, German and Italian air forces. The Republican engineers kept the crossings working under bombardment by repairing and moving the pontoons night after night. The hilltop castle was used as a strongpoint and was heavily shelled and bombed, leaving it semi-ruined. Today it houses an interpretation centre of the Espais de la Batalla de l'Ebre on the logistics of the battle.
look: The partly restored castle with its exhibition, and views of the river crossing points below.
plan: In the town centre; check opening days with the Ebro network or the town tourist office.
disputed: Coordinates are for the town centre (from Wikipedia); the exact position of the castle was not verified.

name: Castell de Montjuïc
text: The fortress above the port was a prison and execution ground for whichever side held Barcelona. In August 1936 the Republican authorities executed rebel generals Manuel Goded and Álvaro Fernández Burriel here after the failed rising of 19 July, and other prisoners followed. After the city fell in January 1939, the Franco regime used the castle as a prison. On 15 October 1940 Lluís Companys, President of the Generalitat, was shot in its moat after a summary court-martial. He had been arrested in France by the Gestapo and handed to Spain. The castle has been in city hands since 2007 and now tells this history.
look: The moat where Companys was shot (a memorial marks the spot), the bastions, and two Civil War-era guns.
plan: By cable car or bus 150; entry fee (free on some Sunday afternoons); allow time for the views and the exhibition on the castle's history.

name: Camp de la Bóta memorial (Fraternitat)
text: The Camp de la Bóta, an old military ground on the shore at the edge of Barcelona, was the main execution site of Francoist repression in the city. It had already been used by the Republican side in 1936 for executions of people convicted of taking part in the military rising. Between 1939 and 1952 about 1,700 people were shot here after court-martial, most of them buried in the Fossar de la Pedrera. The 'Fraternitat' monument by Miquel Navarro, erected in 1992, remembers them.
look: A tall modern sculpture near the Fòrum esplanade, with a plaque; nothing survives of the camp itself.
plan: Beside the Ronda Litoral near the Fòrum; free; tram T4 or metro L4 (El Maresme | Fòrum).
disputed: The plaque gives 1,734 people shot; other counts give 1,717 executions in Barcelona for 1939–52. The number of Republican-period executions here in 1936 is not well documented.

name: Telefónica building & Plaça de Catalunya (May Days 1937)
text: On 3 May 1937 Catalan police under Eusebio Rodríguez Salas tried to take the Telefónica exchange from the CNT workers' committee that had run it since July 1936. The anarchists opened fire, and within hours barricades went up across Barcelona. The CNT and POUM faced the Generalitat, the PSUC communists and the Republican government forces in the 'May Days'. The PSUC headquarters were at the Hotel Colón across the square. After a ceasefire and the arrival of Assault Guards from Valencia, the government took control of public order in Catalonia. The events led to the suppression of the POUM and the kidnapping and murder of Andreu Nin.
look: The Telefónica building (1926–28) still faces the square, though its dome was removed in 1949; the Hotel Colón stood on the Passeig de Gràcia corner and was later replaced.
plan: Free, always visible; combine with the Poliorama and Rambla stop (5 minutes' walk).
disputed: Deaths in the May Days: contemporary press reported about 500 killed; recent research puts it at about 218–235 in Barcelona.

name: Teatre Poliorama, La Rambla (Orwell's rooftop)
text: George Orwell, on leave from the POUM militia on the Aragon front, spent the May Days of 1937 on the roof of the Poliorama cinema (Rambla 115) guarding the POUM executive building across the Rambla, as he describes in 'Homage to Catalonia'. The Rambla, Plaça de Catalunya and the old city were divided by barricades between CNT/POUM and government/PSUC forces. A month later the POUM was outlawed and Orwell escaped from Spain as its members were being arrested. A small square in the Gothic Quarter, Plaça de George Orwell, now bears his name.
look: The building of the Reial Acadèmia de Ciències i Arts with the Poliorama theatre, its façade and clock tower much as Orwell knew them.
plan: Free, visible from La Rambla; the theatre is open only for performances.
disputed: Plaça de George Orwell coordinates were not verified and it is not given as a separate stop.

name: Barcelona Cathedral – memorial to clergy killed in 1936
text: In the first months after the military rising was defeated in Barcelona on 19–20 July 1936, a wave of revolutionary violence swept the Republican zone. Priests, monks, nuns and Catholic laypeople were among its main victims, and many churches were burned. Most of the killings were carried out by militia patrols and 'control committees' outside any legal process; the Generalitat and the Republican government gradually reined them in from late 1936. A chapel in the cathedral precinct remembers the clergy of the diocese who were killed, some of whom have since been beatified.
look: A memorial chapel and plaques in the cathedral precinct on Carrer del Bisbe.
plan: Inside or next to the cathedral; entry to parts of the cathedral requires a ticket outside worship hours; be respectful during services.
disputed: Nationwide, about 6,800 clergy were killed in the Republican zone (A. Montero's count). The exact location and form of this chapel should be checked on site.

name: Camp d'Aviació de la Sénia
text: The Republican Army built this airfield in 1936–37 with Soviet machinery. After the Nationalist drive to the sea in April 1938 cut the Republic in two, it was captured and used by Nationalist squadrons and the German Condor Legion. From here they flew against Valencia and over the Battle of the Ebro. It was abandoned after the war. The surviving command house now holds the Centre d'Aviació Històrica de la Sénia, with aircraft and aeronautical items, and the site is protected as local cultural heritage.
look: The original command building with the museum, aircraft on display, and the flat former landing field.
plan: On the La Sénia–Ulldecona road (Camí dels Plans); museum opening is limited, mostly at weekends; check before going.

name: Els Monjos airfield – Refugi del Serral
text: The Republican air force had a military airfield near Els Monjos in the Penedès, part of a network of Catalan fields that sheltered fighters and bombers from 1937. Because the airfield made the area a bombing target, a shelter for about 120 people was dug in 1937 next to the Serral farmhouse, which was used as a barracks. Its brick-vaulted galleries and three ventilation shafts survive and can be visited as part of the municipality's airfield memory route. It is a rare surviving piece of the Republic's wartime air infrastructure in the Penedès.
look: A brick barrel-vaulted shelter with ventilation shafts beside the Serral farmhouse; remains of the airfield landscape around.
plan: On the path from Sardinyola to Els Monjos; ask Santa Margarida i els Monjos town hall about guided visits to the shelter and airfield route.
disputed: The name and opening hours of the airfield interpretation centre were not verified.

name: Mont de Conques – Pallars front strongholds
text: After the Nationalist Aragon offensive of spring 1938 the front in western Catalonia settled along the Segre and Noguera Pallaresa rivers. The Nationalists held bridgeheads at Tremp, Balaguer and Seròs. Mont de Conques, near Isona in the Conca de Tremp, was fortified by the Nationalists and attacked several times by the Republicans, especially in their May 1938 offensive against the Tremp and Balaguer bridgeheads, which failed at high cost. The line held until the Nationalist Catalonia offensive of December 1938. Republican positions such as the La Posa bunker at Abella de la Conca faced it across the valley.
look: Nationalist concrete positions and trenches on the hill; the Republican La Posa bunker at Abella de la Conca (42.13311, 1.07633) is nearby.
plan: Rough tracks from Conques (Camí Vell d'Isona); walking boots needed; no facilities.

name: La Vajol & Coll de Lli – exile crossing
text: In the last days of the Republic in Catalonia, the tiny border village of La Vajol and its surroundings sheltered members of the government and treasures evacuated from Barcelona. On 5 February 1939 President Manuel Azaña walked across the frontier at the Coll de Lli into France. Lluís Companys and the Basque president José Antonio Aguirre crossed the same day. Thousands of refugees used the same mountain paths. A monument to the exile marks the route. Paintings from the Prado and other evacuated collections were also stored in this area before being taken on to Geneva.
look: The exile monument and waymarked mountain paths towards the Coll de Lli and the French border.
plan: Small mountain village north of Agullana, reached by a winding road; the walk to the border is on forest tracks, so ask at La Jonquera's MUME for route details.
disputed: Coordinates are the village centre only; the monument and Coll de Lli positions were not verified. Details of the route taken by each leader vary between accounts.

name: Crypt of the Tercio de Montserrat, Montserrat
text: The Tercio de Requetés de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat was a unit of Catalan Carlist volunteers who fought on the Nationalist side, many of them having escaped from Republican Catalonia. It suffered heavy losses at Codo (Aragon) in August 1937 and in the Battle of the Ebro, including at Quatre Camins near Vilalba dels Arcs. Its dead were brought to a crypt at the monastery of Montserrat, Catalonia's national shrine. The crypt is a reminder that Catalan society was divided by the war.
look: A mausoleum or crypt with the names of the unit's dead, within the Montserrat monastery complex.
plan: In the monastery precinct (rack railway or cable car from the Llobregat valley); access to the crypt may be restricted, so ask at the information office.

name: Portbou – Walter Benjamin memorial 'Passatges'
text: Portbou, the railway frontier town, was one of the main crossing points of the Retirada in February 1939. Eighteen months later the flow ran the other way: refugees from Nazi-occupied France tried to reach Spain and Portugal. On 26 September 1940 the German-Jewish philosopher Walter Benjamin, turned back by the Spanish authorities after crossing the Pyrenees on foot, took his own life here. Dani Karavan's memorial 'Passatges' (1994) is a steel corridor descending towards the sea. It belongs to the story of exile rather than to the Civil War itself.
look: Karavan's steel stairway descending towards the sea beside the cemetery, Benjamin's memorial stone, and the view over the bay.
plan: Free; a short walk up from the station to the cemetery; combine with the border crossing to Cerbère.

name: Bunquers de Martinet (Línea P)
text: These are not Civil War works but its aftermath. After the Republican guerrilla incursion into the Val d'Aran in October 1944, and fearing an Allied or exile invasion, the Franco regime secretly built the 'Línea P' (Pirineos) fortification line. It had thousands of concrete bunkers from the Cap de Creus to the Basque coast and was never used in combat. At Martinet in the Cerdanya a group of bunkers has been restored and opened as an interpretation park. It shows how far the regime's post-war isolation and fears shaped the frontier.
look: Restored machine-gun and anti-tank bunkers with connecting trenches, and an interpretation centre.
plan: Off the LV-4055 at Martinet; guided visits must be booked (bunquersmartinet.net, tel. +34 648 141 070).
